props.title: Little Manhattan
props.initialSlug: 11-year-old finds first love in NYC's Upper West Side

sections.content: Little Manhattan captures first love's bittersweet intensity through 10-year-old Gabe's crush on his karate classmate Rosemary. Set against Manhattan's Upper West Side, it shares DNA with classic New York romances like When Harry Met Sally (1989) and You've Got Mail (1998), but through a child's pure perspective. Josh Hutcherson's breakthrough performance nails the awkward vulnerability of preteen romance, while Charlie Ray brings natural charm to Rosemary. Director Mark Levin uses the city as a magical playground, making Central Park and Riverside Drive feel as epic as Gabe's emotions.

sections.content: The film excels at showing how kids process adult relationships through their limited experience. Gabe watches his parents' divorce unfold while experiencing his own heartache, echoing themes from The Parent Trap (1998) and Mrs. Doubtfire (1993). But unlike those broader family comedies, Little Manhattan stays grounded in authentic preteen emotions. The voiceover narration works because it captures Gabe's genuine confusion and wonder rather than trying for adult-level insights.

Coming-of-age stories often focus on teens, but Little Manhattan joins rare films like My Girl (1991) and Now and Then (1995) in exploring the specific moment when kids first realize romantic feelings exist. The karate classes provide a perfect backdrop for physical awkwardness and shifting relationship dynamics. Like The Sandlot (1993), it understands how childhood spaces become charged with new meaning during these transitions. SUBHEAD: New York as a Character

sections.content: Few films capture Manhattan through a child's eyes like this one. While Home Alone 2: Lost in New York (1992) used the city as an adventure playground, Little Manhattan makes it an intimate emotional landscape. Every location - from Gray's Papaya to the Natural History Museum - reflects Gabe's expanding world. The film joins Harriet the Spy (1996) in showing how kids claim city spaces as their own private kingdoms.
